title: Create NCR and CAPA SharePoint lists with PnP.PowerShell, with a -WhatIf dry run
summary: A repeatable PnP.PowerShell script that creates NCR and CAPA lists with columns and versioning, skips what exists, and supports -WhatIf through ShouldProcess. No secrets, interactive sign-in with your own app registration.
body:
# Create the NCR and CAPA lists in SharePoint with PnP.PowerShell

Many plants start nonconformance and corrective action tracking in a spreadsheet and outgrow it within a quarter. A pair of SharePoint lists is a sensible next step: one row per nonconformance report (NCR), one row per corrective or preventive action (CAPA), both with versioning on and the same columns every time. This script creates both lists with their columns, repeatably, on any quality site. Run it with `-WhatIf` first: it connects, reads what exists and prints what it would create, without changing anything.

The lists are a data foundation. Who may open an NCR, which dispositions are allowed, how a part is released after rework and what your customer must be told are defined in your quality system, not in this script. In aviation, disposition of a part and the release to service stay with authorised people under your procedures.

## Prerequisites and version

- PnP.PowerShell installed (`Install-Module PnP.PowerShell`). Check the module's current requirements for the PowerShell version before you install; recent versions need PowerShell 7.
- An Entra ID app registration that you own for interactive login. The documentation of `Connect-PnPOnline` states that your own app and `-ClientId` are required for interactive login (from 9 September 2024) and points to `Register-PnPEntraIDApp` for the registration. You can also set the environment variable `ENTRAID_CLIENT_ID` and omit the parameter. Read the current guidance, it changes.
- The account must be a site owner (or have permission to create lists) on the target site.
- Cmdlets used: `Connect-PnPOnline`, `Get-PnPList`, `New-PnPList`, `Set-PnPList`, `Get-PnPField`, `Add-PnPField`. `New-PnPList` and `Add-PnPField` do not document a `-WhatIf` switch, so the script implements its own through `SupportsShouldProcess` and `$PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess`. Only `New-PnPList`, `Set-PnPList` and `Add-PnPField` change anything, and each sits behind a `ShouldProcess` check; the connect call is explicitly shielded from `-WhatIf`, because a dry run still has to sign in and read.

## Script

```powershell
<#
.SYNOPSIS
  Creates the NCR and CAPA lists with columns and versioning on a SharePoint site.
.EXAMPLE
  .\New-QualityLists.ps1 -SiteUrl https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/quality -ClientId <app-id> -WhatIf
#>
[CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess = $true)]
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$SiteUrl,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$ClientId,
    [string]$NcrListTitle  = 'NCR',
    [string]$CapaListTitle = 'CAPA'
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

# 1. Connect interactively. No secrets in the script.
# A dry run still has to connect and read, so keep -WhatIf away from the connect call.
$savedWhatIf = $WhatIfPreference
$WhatIfPreference = $false
try     { Connect-PnPOnline -Url $SiteUrl -Interactive -ClientId $ClientId }
finally { $WhatIfPreference = $savedWhatIf }

# 2. Column definitions. Title holds the NCR number or the CAPA number.
$ncrFields = @(
    @{ Name = 'PartNumber';   Display = 'Part number';    Type = 'Text';     Required = $true },
    @{ Name = 'PartRevision'; Display = 'Part revision';  Type = 'Text' },
    @{ Name = 'WorkOrder';    Display = 'Work order';     Type = 'Text' },
    @{ Name = 'Supplier';     Display = 'Supplier';       Type = 'Text' },
    @{ Name = 'Description';  Display = 'Description';    Type = 'Note';     Required = $true },
    @{ Name = 'Severity';     Display = 'Severity';       Type = 'Choice';   Choices = @('Minor', 'Major', 'Critical') },
    @{ Name = 'DetectedOn';   Display = 'Detected on';    Type = 'DateTime' },
    @{ Name = 'DetectedBy';   Display = 'Detected by';    Type = 'User' },
    @{ Name = 'Disposition';  Display = 'Disposition';    Type = 'Choice';   Choices = @('Pending', 'Rework', 'Repair', 'Scrap', 'Return to supplier', 'Use as is with approval') },
    @{ Name = 'NcrStatus';    Display = 'Status';         Type = 'Choice';   Choices = @('New', 'Under review', 'Awaiting disposition', 'Closed') }
)
$capaFields = @(
    @{ Name = 'NcrNumber';    Display = 'NCR number';     Type = 'Text';     Required = $true },
    @{ Name = 'ActionText';   Display = 'Action';         Type = 'Note';     Required = $true },
    @{ Name = 'ActionOwner';  Display = 'Owner';          Type = 'User' },
    @{ Name = 'DueDate';      Display = 'Due date';       Type = 'DateTime' },
    @{ Name = 'VerifyOn';     Display = 'Verify on';      Type = 'DateTime' },
    @{ Name = 'Effectiveness'; Display = 'Effectiveness'; Type = 'Choice';   Choices = @('Not yet verified', 'Effective', 'Not effective') },
    @{ Name = 'CapaStatus';   Display = 'Status';         Type = 'Choice';   Choices = @('Open', 'In progress', 'In verification', 'Closed') }
)

function Initialize-QualityList {
    [CmdletBinding(SupportsShouldProcess = $true)]
    param(
        [string]$Title,
        [object[]]$Fields
    )

    $list = Get-PnPList -Identity $Title
    if (-not $list) {
        if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess($SiteUrl, "Create list '$Title'")) {
            $list = New-PnPList -Title $Title -Template GenericList -Url "Lists/$Title" -OnQuickLaunch
            Set-PnPList -Identity $Title -EnableVersioning $true
            Write-Host "Created list '$Title' with versioning on." -ForegroundColor Green
        }
        else {
            Write-Host "Would create list '$Title'." -ForegroundColor Yellow
        }
    }
    else {
        Write-Host "List '$Title' exists, only missing columns will be added." -ForegroundColor Cyan
    }

    $existing = @()
    if ($list) { $existing = @(Get-PnPField -List $Title | Select-Object -ExpandProperty InternalName) }

    foreach ($f in $Fields) {
        if ($existing -contains $f.Name) {
            Write-Host "  column $($f.Name) exists, skipped"
            continue
        }
        if ($PSCmdlet.ShouldProcess("$Title", "Add column $($f.Name) ($($f.Type))")) {
            $p = @{
                List          = $Title
                DisplayName   = $f.Display
                InternalName  = $f.Name
                Type          = $f.Type
                AddToDefaultView = $true
            }
            if ($f.Required) { $p.Required = $true }
            if ($f.Choices)  { $p.Choices  = $f.Choices }
            Add-PnPField @p | Out-Null
            Write-Host "  column $($f.Name) added" -ForegroundColor Green
        }
    }
}

Initialize-QualityList -Title $NcrListTitle  -Fields $ncrFields
Initialize-QualityList -Title $CapaListTitle -Fields $capaFields

Write-Host 'Done. Review the lists in the browser before you give users access.'
```

## How to run

1. Dry run: `.\New-QualityLists.ps1 -SiteUrl <site url> -ClientId <app id> -WhatIf`. It signs in and reads, then prints lines such as "What if: Performing the operation "Create list 'NCR'" on target ...". Nothing is created. On a site where the lists do not exist yet it also prints every column as "would add", because it cannot read the columns of a list that is not there.
2. Real run without `-WhatIf` on a test site first. The script is safe to run again; it skips lists and columns that already exist and only adds missing columns.
3. Open both lists and check the column order, the default view and the permissions. New lists inherit the permissions of the site; for a quality site that is usually wrong, see the permission report script in this library.

## Worked example (invented data)

A first run on an empty test site: the NCR list gets 10 columns and the CAPA list 7, which means 17 `Add-PnPField` calls plus 2 list creations and 2 versioning updates, 21 operations in total. A second run prints "List 'NCR' exists" and "column ... exists, skipped" 17 times and changes nothing. If someone deleted the column `Severity` in between, the next run adds exactly that column and nothing else. A first NCR could then be: Title "NCR-2026-088", PartNumber "PN-4711" (an invented number), Severity Major, NcrStatus New. One CAPA row with NcrNumber "NCR-2026-088", Owner, DueDate and Effectiveness "Not yet verified" links to it by the number.

## How to adapt

- Column names and choices: change the two arrays. Keep internal names stable, because flows, apps and reports refer to them. Display names can change later; internal names cannot.
- Lookup from CAPA to NCR instead of a text number: that needs a lookup column definition, which `Add-PnPField` with a plain type does not cover in this script. Keep the text key, or add the lookup in the browser after the run.
- Version limits: `Set-PnPList` has `-MajorVersions` to limit stored versions. Set it according to your retention rules, not to a number from a template.
- Content types, attachments and approval: `Set-PnPList` supports `-EnableContentTypes`, `-EnableAttachments` and more; add them to the version line if you need them.
- Tenants with a naming convention for lists: change the title parameters.

## Common mistakes

- Running the script with an account that is only a member of the site. List creation needs more than member rights.
- Forgetting the `-ClientId` and getting a login error. The module needs your own app registration for interactive login.
- Changing internal names after flows exist. The flow breaks silently.
- Using Choice values with typos in a later flow filter. Copy the strings from the arrays above.
- Treating `Status` as workflow. The column stores a value; the rules that decide who may change it (and when) must come from permissions and from a flow.

## Privacy and security

- NCR rows can contain customer names, part numbers and supplier information. Give the list unique permissions and keep the owners group small.
- `DetectedBy` and `Owner` are person columns. If you evaluate NCRs by person, involve the works council or data protection officer first; evaluate by process and cause.
- The script stores nothing: no secret, no token. Do not paste one into it. For unattended runs use a certificate-based app registration and protect the certificate.
- Do not use the script in a production site before the site owner has agreed the structure.

title: Export SharePoint document version history to CSV for an audit with PnP.PowerShell
summary: Read-only script that lists current and earlier versions of every file in a library with editor, date, size and comment, writes a CSV and a SHA-256 checksum, and explains which properties to verify in your tenant.
body:
# Export document version history from a SharePoint library for an audit

Before an AS9100 or customer audit somebody usually spends a day opening version history windows to show that a procedure changed under control: which versions exist, who saved them, when, and with what comment. This script does it for a whole library or a folder in one run and writes a CSV plus a checksum file. It is read-only: it changes no document, no setting and no permission.

What counts as a controlled revision is defined by your quality system (approval, release, effectivity), not by SharePoint's version numbers. The export is supporting evidence of what the platform recorded. It does not prove approval by itself.

## Prerequisites and version

- PnP.PowerShell (check the current module requirements, recent versions need PowerShell 7) and an Entra ID app registration of your own for interactive sign-in. The `Connect-PnPOnline` documentation says your own app and `-ClientId` are required for interactive login; the environment variable `ENTRAID_CLIENT_ID` can replace the parameter.
- Read access to the library. Versioning must have been on when the edits were made; versions may be trimmed by library version limits or retention rules, so the export shows what still exists.
- Cmdlets used (all confirmed in the PnP.PowerShell documentation): `Connect-PnPOnline`, `Get-PnPListItem` with `-List`, `-PageSize`, `-Fields`, `Get-PnPFileVersion` with `-Url`.

## Script

```powershell
<#
.SYNOPSIS
  Exports the version history of all files in a library (read-only).
.EXAMPLE
  .\Export-DocumentVersions.ps1 -SiteUrl https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/quality -ClientId <app-id> -Library 'Controlled Documents' -MaxFiles 5
#>
[CmdletBinding()]
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$SiteUrl,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$ClientId,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$Library,
    [string]$PathContains = '',
    [int]$MaxFiles = 0,
    [string]$OutputPath = ".\DocumentVersions_$(Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd_HHmm').csv"
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

Connect-PnPOnline -Url $SiteUrl -Interactive -ClientId $ClientId

$fields = 'FileLeafRef', 'FileRef', 'FSObjType', '_UIVersionString', 'Modified', 'Editor'
$items  = Get-PnPListItem -List $Library -PageSize 500 -Fields $fields |
    Where-Object { $_.FieldValues['FSObjType'] -eq 0 }

if ($PathContains) {
    $items = $items | Where-Object { $_.FieldValues['FileRef'] -like "*$PathContains*" }
}
if ($MaxFiles -gt 0) {
    $items = $items | Select-Object -First $MaxFiles
}

$rows  = New-Object System.Collections.Generic.List[object]
$total = @($items).Count
$n     = 0

foreach ($item in $items) {
    $n++
    $fileRef = $item.FieldValues['FileRef']
    Write-Progress -Activity 'Reading versions' -Status $fileRef -PercentComplete (100 * $n / [math]::Max($total, 1))

    # Current version: taken from the list item, because the version collection holds earlier versions.
    $editor = $item.FieldValues['Editor']
    $rows.Add([pscustomobject]@{
        File            = $item.FieldValues['FileLeafRef']
        Path            = $fileRef
        VersionLabel    = $item.FieldValues['_UIVersionString']
        IsCurrent       = $true
        SavedOn         = $item.FieldValues['Modified']
        SavedBy         = if ($editor) { $editor.LookupValue } else { '' }
        SizeBytes       = $null
        CheckInComment  = ''
    })

    try {
        $versions = @(Get-PnPFileVersion -Url $fileRef)
    }
    catch {
        Write-Warning "Could not read versions of $fileRef : $($_.Exception.Message)"
        continue
    }

    foreach ($v in $versions) {
        $by = if ($v.CreatedBy) { $v.CreatedBy.Title } else { '' }
        $rows.Add([pscustomobject]@{
            File            = $item.FieldValues['FileLeafRef']
            Path            = $fileRef
            VersionLabel    = $v.VersionLabel
            IsCurrent       = $false
            SavedOn         = $v.Created
            SavedBy         = $by
            SizeBytes       = $v.Size
            CheckInComment  = $v.CheckInComment
        })
    }
}

$rows | Sort-Object Path, @{ Expression = 'SavedOn'; Descending = $true } |
    Export-Csv -Path $OutputPath -NoTypeInformation -Encoding UTF8

# Checksum so the evidence file can be shown to be unchanged later
$hash = Get-FileHash -Path $OutputPath -Algorithm SHA256
"$($hash.Hash)  $(Split-Path -Leaf $OutputPath)" | Set-Content -Path "$OutputPath.sha256" -Encoding ASCII

Write-Host "Files: $total, version rows: $($rows.Count)" -ForegroundColor Cyan
Write-Host "CSV: $OutputPath"
Write-Host "SHA-256 written to $OutputPath.sha256"
```

## How to run

1. Start with `-MaxFiles 5` to test the sign-in, the columns and the runtime. The script only reads.
2. Use `-PathContains 'Procedures'` to limit to a folder path fragment.
3. Open the CSV in Excel, filter on one file and compare with the version history window in the browser for that file. Do this for at least two files before you trust the export.
4. Store the CSV and the `.sha256` file in the audit folder, not in the document library.

## Property notes (check in your tenant)

- `Get-PnPFileVersion` writes the version objects of the file. The documentation page lists no property names; the cmdlet source loads the versions together with `CreatedBy`, `SnapshotDate` and `ExpirationDate`. The script uses `VersionLabel`, `Created`, `Size`, `CheckInComment` and `CreatedBy.Title`, which are properties of the SharePoint file version object. Run `Get-PnPFileVersion -Url <path> | Get-Member` once on your tenant to confirm they exist and are filled.
- The `Get-PnPFileVersion` documentation says it retrieves the previous versions of a file and does not retrieve the current version. The current version is therefore read from the list item (`_UIVersionString`), and the script adds it as a separate row. If you still see the same version label twice in your tenant, remove the extra row logic.
- `Editor` is a person field. In the list item values it appears as a lookup value object; the script reads `LookupValue`.

## Worked example (invented data)

A test library has 3 files. File A has 4 earlier versions, file B has 1, file C has 0. The script writes (1 + 4) + (1 + 1) + (1 + 0) = 8 rows: three current rows (IsCurrent true) and five earlier versions. With `-MaxFiles 2` and files A and B returned first, the CSV would hold 5 + 2 = 7 rows. Sorting by path and by date puts the newest version first for each file. The `.sha256` file contains one line with the hash and the CSV file name; after the audit, `Get-FileHash` on the stored CSV must give the same value, otherwise the file was changed.

## How to adapt

- Another identity or unattended run: use app-only login with a certificate; see the `Connect-PnPOnline` documentation for certificate parameters and keep the certificate out of the repository.
- Add columns: extend `$fields` with your own internal column names (revision, document owner, status) and write them into the row object. Check internal names with `Get-PnPField -List <library>`.
- Large libraries: `-PageSize 500` fetches 500 items per request. Expect throttling on tens of thousands of files; run outside working hours and in batches with `-PathContains`.
- Comment export: if your process uses check-in comments as the change description, the `CheckInComment` column is the one the auditor wants; train people to write it.

## Common mistakes

- Reading `Modified` of the current item as "date of approval". It is the last save.
- Forgetting that trimmed versions are gone. The auditor will ask why version 3 is missing; the answer is in the version limit setting.
- Exporting into a shared folder and leaving it there.
- Running the script against a library with millions of items from a laptop on a bad connection, then repeating it three times.
- Sorting the CSV in Excel and breaking the hash. Hash the original; work on a copy.

## Privacy and security

- The CSV lists who saved what and when. That is employee data. Use it for the audit purpose, share it with the auditor only as needed, and delete it after the retention period you agreed.
- Do not store tokens or secrets in the script. Interactive sign-in means the session token stays with the module.
- In aerospace and defence environments, export-controlled or customer-restricted documents may be in the library. File names alone can be sensitive; check before you send the CSV outside the company.

title: Permission report for a SharePoint quality library with PnP.PowerShell and Graph PowerShell
summary: Read-only report of role assignments on a library, optional expansion of SharePoint groups, broad-access flags, item-level unique permissions and Entra group member counts through Microsoft Graph PowerShell.
body:
# Permission report for a SharePoint quality library with PnP.PowerShell and Microsoft Graph PowerShell

The quality library holds work instructions, procedures, audit evidence and sometimes customer drawings. Over the years people were added to groups, a folder was shared with a supplier, an item got unique permissions "just for the audit", and nobody knows any more who can edit what. This script lists who has access to the library, with which roles, whether the library has its own permissions, which principals look too broad (Everyone, external users, Full Control), and optionally which items break inheritance. For Entra groups it can add the number of members through Microsoft Graph PowerShell. The script only reads.

The report is the starting point for a conversation with the library owner. Access decisions remain with the owner and the quality manager. In aerospace and defence environments, restricted or export-controlled content may require specific rules on who may have access; check your security officer's requirements.

## Prerequisites and version

- PnP.PowerShell (check the current requirements; recent versions need PowerShell 7) and your own Entra ID app registration for interactive sign-in; `Connect-PnPOnline` documentation states that `-ClientId` is required for interactive login, or set `ENTRAID_CLIENT_ID`.
- For the optional group count: the Microsoft Graph PowerShell SDK (module `Microsoft.Graph.Groups` and `Microsoft.Graph.Authentication`) and a delegated permission for group members. The `Get-MgGroupMember` page lists GroupMember.ReadBasic.All as the least privileged option and GroupMember.Read.All further up; the script requests GroupMember.Read.All, and you can test the ReadBasic variant if your tenant prefers it. Admin consent may be required. The cmdlet returns direct members only (not transitive), so a nested group counts as one member.
- Permission to read role assignments on the library (site owner or similar).
- Cmdlets used and confirmed in the documentation: `Connect-PnPOnline`, `Get-PnPList`, `Get-PnPProperty`, `Get-PnPGroupMember`, `Get-PnPListItem`, `Connect-MgGraph -Scopes -NoWelcome`, `Get-MgGroupMember -GroupId -All`.

## Script

```powershell
<#
.SYNOPSIS
  Reports who has access to a library (read-only).
.EXAMPLE
  .\Get-LibraryPermissionReport.ps1 -SiteUrl https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/quality -ClientId <app-id> -Library 'Controlled Documents' -ExpandGroups
#>
[CmdletBinding()]
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$SiteUrl,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$ClientId,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$Library,
    [switch]$ExpandGroups,
    [switch]$CountEntraGroupMembers,
    [switch]$IncludeItemLevel,
    [string]$OutputPath = ".\LibraryPermissions_$(Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd_HHmm').csv"
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

Connect-PnPOnline -Url $SiteUrl -Interactive -ClientId $ClientId

if ($CountEntraGroupMembers) {
    Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'GroupMember.Read.All' -NoWelcome
}

function Get-Flags {
    param([string]$LoginName, [string]$Roles)
    $flags = @()
    # Claim patterns below are commonly seen, check them in your tenant
    if ($LoginName -like '*spo-grid-all-users*' -or $LoginName -like 'c:0(.s|true*') { $flags += 'Broad (Everyone)' }
    if ($LoginName -like '*#ext#*') { $flags += 'External user' }
    if ($Roles -match 'Full Control') { $flags += 'Full Control' }
    if ($Roles -match 'Full Control|Edit|Contribute') { $flags += 'Can change content' }
    return ($flags -join '; ')
}

function Get-EntraGroupCount {
    param([string]$LoginName)
    if (-not $CountEntraGroupMembers) { return $null }
    $m = [regex]::Match($LoginName, '[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-([0-9a-fA-F]{4}-){3}[0-9a-fA-F]{12}')
    if (-not $m.Success) { return $null }
    try { return @(Get-MgGroupMember -GroupId $m.Value -All).Count }
    catch { return -1 }   # -1 = lookup failed, for example not an Entra group
}

function Get-RoleRows {
    param($Securable, [string]$ScopeName, [string]$Path)
    $rows = @()
    Get-PnPProperty -ClientObject $Securable -Property RoleAssignments | Out-Null
    foreach ($ra in $Securable.RoleAssignments) {
        Get-PnPProperty -ClientObject $ra -Property RoleDefinitionBindings, Member | Out-Null
        $roles = ($ra.RoleDefinitionBindings | ForEach-Object { $_.Name }) -join ', '
        $login = $ra.Member.LoginName
        $rows += [pscustomobject]@{
            Scope         = $ScopeName
            Path          = $Path
            PrincipalType = [string]$ra.Member.PrincipalType
            Principal     = $ra.Member.Title
            LoginName     = $login
            Roles         = $roles
            MemberCount   = $null
            EntraMembers  = Get-EntraGroupCount -LoginName $login
            Flags         = Get-Flags -LoginName $login -Roles $roles
        }
        if ($ExpandGroups -and [string]$ra.Member.PrincipalType -eq 'SharePointGroup') {
            $members = @(Get-PnPGroupMember -Group $ra.Member.Title)
            $rows[-1].MemberCount = $members.Count
            foreach ($u in $members) {
                $rows += [pscustomobject]@{
                    Scope         = "$ScopeName (via group)"
                    Path          = $Path
                    PrincipalType = 'GroupMember'
                    Principal     = $u.Title
                    LoginName     = $u.LoginName
                    Roles         = $roles
                    MemberCount   = $null
                    EntraMembers  = $null
                    Flags         = Get-Flags -LoginName $u.LoginName -Roles $roles
                }
            }
        }
    }
    return $rows
}

$list = Get-PnPList -Identity $Library -ThrowExceptionIfListNotFound
Get-PnPProperty -ClientObject $list -Property HasUniqueRoleAssignments | Out-Null
Write-Host "Library '$Library' has unique permissions: $($list.HasUniqueRoleAssignments)" -ForegroundColor Cyan

$report = @()
$report += Get-RoleRows -Securable $list -ScopeName 'Library' -Path $Library

if ($IncludeItemLevel) {
    $items = Get-PnPListItem -List $list -PageSize 500 -Fields 'FileRef'
    foreach ($item in $items) {
        Get-PnPProperty -ClientObject $item -Property HasUniqueRoleAssignments | Out-Null
        if ($item.HasUniqueRoleAssignments) {
            $report += Get-RoleRows -Securable $item -ScopeName 'Item' -Path $item.FieldValues['FileRef']
        }
    }
}

$report | Export-Csv -Path $OutputPath -NoTypeInformation -Encoding UTF8
$report | Where-Object { $_.Flags } | Group-Object Flags | Select-Object Name, Count | Format-Table -AutoSize
Write-Host "Report written to $OutputPath" -ForegroundColor Green
```

## How to run

1. First run without switches: it reads only the library level and takes seconds.
2. Add `-ExpandGroups` to list the members of SharePoint groups that have access.
3. Add `-CountEntraGroupMembers` to see how many members the Entra groups behind the claims have. This signs in to Microsoft Graph PowerShell interactively. The claim format that carries the group id is commonly seen but tenant specific; a result of -1 means the lookup did not work for that principal.
4. Add `-IncludeItemLevel` only on a test library first. It asks the server per item whether it has unique permissions, which is slow on large libraries and can run into throttling.

## Property notes (check in your tenant)

- `Get-PnPProperty -ClientObject <object> -Property <names>` is documented to load properties of a client object. The properties used here (`RoleAssignments`, `HasUniqueRoleAssignments`, `RoleDefinitionBindings`, `Member`) belong to the SharePoint client object model; the documentation page for the cmdlet shows other examples, so verify with one library that the values are filled.
- Claim patterns for "Everyone" and for guests in the flag function are commonly seen forms. Compare them with real values in the LoginName column of your first report before you rely on the flags.
- Role names (Full Control, Edit, Contribute) can be renamed or customised in your tenant; the flag text matches the English default names. `Get-PnPGroupMember` is documented to return the users of a SharePoint group and its output type is the SharePoint `User` object, so `Title` and `LoginName` exist; the script passes the group by its title.

## Worked example (invented data)

A library has unique permissions. The report shows 5 rows at library level: the site owners group (Full Control), the site members group (Edit), the visitors group (Read), an Entra security group "Quality-Editors" (Contribute) and "Supplier-Portal-Guests" (Read). With `-ExpandGroups` the members group expands to 24 people, the owners to 3. With `-CountEntraGroupMembers`, "Quality-Editors" shows 12 members and the guest group 7. Result: up to 3 + 24 + 12 = 39 people can change content (overlaps between groups are possible), while only the quality team of 12 is intended to. The members group is the finding. The follow-up is a decision of the library owner: split the group, or move the content to a library with its own permission group. The numbers are invented; the point is the arithmetic from role to people.

## How to adapt

- Several libraries: loop over a list of titles and append to one CSV.
- Compare over time: keep the CSVs of each quarter and compare `Principal` and `Roles`; new rows are the changes.
- Sharing links: this script reports role assignments, not sharing links. Review links separately in SharePoint admin tooling or with Graph.
- Only flags: filter the CSV for rows with a flag and send them to the owner.

## Common mistakes

- Reading the report as proof that nobody else has access. Site collection admins and tenant admins are not shown as role assignments.
- Giving the app registration broad site permissions when a person with owner rights could run it interactively.
- Running `-IncludeItemLevel` on a library with 100,000 items and then starting it again after a timeout.
- Treating "Edit" membership as bad in itself. The question is whether the right people have it.
- Emailing the CSV to a large list; it contains names.

## Privacy and security

- The report contains names and login names. Share it with the library owner only, store it with the audit file, and delete it per your retention rules.
- Ask the works council or data protection officer if reports like this are part of a regular review process.
- No secrets in the script. For unattended runs, use certificate-based app-only access and restrict the app to the sites it needs.

title: Check retention labels, review dates and library settings of controlled documents with PnP.PowerShell
summary: Read-only check of a document library: versioning settings, files without a retention label or with a label outside your allowed list, overdue review dates and approval status, with a CSV and counts per issue.
body:
# Check retention labels and library settings of controlled documents with PnP.PowerShell

Controlled documents (work instructions, procedures, forms, supplier certificates) should sit in libraries that behave the same way: versioning on, no stray unlabelled files, only approved retention labels, and a review date that is not overdue. Auditors ask for exactly this, and nobody wants to check 4,000 files by hand. This script reads a library and reports per file whether it carries a retention label, whether that label is on your list of allowed labels, whether an approval status or a review date is out of order, and how the library itself is configured. It is read-only: it applies no label and changes no setting.

The script finds gaps. Which label applies to which document type, how long records are kept and what the label does at the end of the period are decisions of your records manager and quality system, made in Microsoft Purview, not in this script. In aviation, record retention periods come from regulation, customers and your own procedures; check them there, not here.

## Prerequisites and version

- PnP.PowerShell (check the current module requirements, recent versions need PowerShell 7) and your own Entra ID app registration for interactive sign-in. The `Connect-PnPOnline` documentation says `-ClientId` is required for interactive login; the environment variable `ENTRAID_CLIENT_ID` can replace it.
- Read access to the library.
- Retention labels already published to the site by your compliance team. The label name of a file is commonly stored in a column with the internal name `_ComplianceTag`, which holds the name of the applied label. I could not confirm that internal name on a Microsoft Learn page, so treat it as unverified. Confirm the column on your library with `Get-PnPField -List '<library>' | Where-Object InternalName -eq '_ComplianceTag'`; the `Get-PnPField` documentation shows the `-List` parameter and listing of fields. If the column does not show up for your tenant, stop and check with your compliance administrator.
- Optional: a review-date column that your own process maintains, for example `NextReview`, and content approval enabled on the library if you want to check approval status (the internal column `_ModerationStatus` exists on libraries with content approval; check the values in your tenant).
- Cmdlets used: `Connect-PnPOnline`, `Get-PnPList` with `-Includes`, `Get-PnPListItem` with `-List`, `-PageSize`, `-Fields`.

## Script

```powershell
<#
.SYNOPSIS
  Reports retention label, approval and review-date gaps of files in a library (read-only).
.EXAMPLE
  .\Test-ControlledDocuments.ps1 -SiteUrl https://contoso.sharepoint.com/sites/quality -ClientId <app-id> -Library 'Controlled Documents' -AllowedLabels 'QMS record 10 years','Procedure current' -ReviewField NextReview
#>
[CmdletBinding()]
param(
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$SiteUrl,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$ClientId,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string]$Library,
    [Parameter(Mandatory = $true)][string[]]$AllowedLabels,
    [string]$ReviewField = '',
    [switch]$CheckApprovalStatus,
    [string]$OutputPath = ".\ControlledDocuments_$(Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMdd_HHmm').csv"
)

$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'

Connect-PnPOnline -Url $SiteUrl -Interactive -ClientId $ClientId

# 1. Library settings
$list = Get-PnPList -Identity $Library -ThrowExceptionIfListNotFound -Includes EnableVersioning, EnableMinorVersions, MajorVersionLimit, ForceCheckout, EnableModeration
[pscustomobject]@{
    Library          = $list.Title
    Versioning       = $list.EnableVersioning
    MinorVersions    = $list.EnableMinorVersions
    MajorVersionLimit = $list.MajorVersionLimit
    ForceCheckout    = $list.ForceCheckout
    ContentApproval  = $list.EnableModeration
} | Format-List

if (-not $list.EnableVersioning) {
    Write-Warning 'Versioning is off on this library. Controlled documents normally need version history.'
}

# 2. Files
$fields = @('FileLeafRef', 'FileRef', 'FSObjType', '_UIVersionString', 'Modified', '_ComplianceTag')
if ($ReviewField)         { $fields += $ReviewField }
if ($CheckApprovalStatus) { $fields += '_ModerationStatus' }

$items = Get-PnPListItem -List $list -PageSize 500 -Fields $fields |
    Where-Object { $_.FieldValues['FSObjType'] -eq 0 }

$today  = (Get-Date).Date
$result = foreach ($item in $items) {
    $fv     = $item.FieldValues
    $label  = [string]$fv['_ComplianceTag']
    $issues = @()

    if ([string]::IsNullOrWhiteSpace($label)) { $issues += 'NoRetentionLabel' }
    elseif ($AllowedLabels -notcontains $label) { $issues += 'LabelNotAllowed' }

    $review = $null
    if ($ReviewField) {
        $review = $fv[$ReviewField]
        if (-not $review) { $issues += 'NoReviewDate' }
        elseif (([datetime]$review).Date -lt $today) { $issues += 'ReviewOverdue' }
    }

    if ($CheckApprovalStatus -and [string]$fv['_ModerationStatus'] -ne '0') {
        $issues += 'NotApproved'   # 0 = approved on libraries with content approval, check in your tenant
    }

    [pscustomobject]@{
        File      = $fv['FileLeafRef']
        Path      = $fv['FileRef']
        Version   = $fv['_UIVersionString']
        Modified  = $fv['Modified']
        Label     = $label
        Review    = $review
        Issues    = ($issues -join '; ')
    }
}

$result | Export-Csv -Path $OutputPath -NoTypeInformation -Encoding UTF8

$total  = @($result).Count
$flagged = @($result | Where-Object { $_.Issues }).Count
Write-Host "Files checked: $total, with at least one issue: $flagged" -ForegroundColor Cyan
$result | Where-Object { $_.Issues } | ForEach-Object { $_.Issues -split '; ' } |
    Group-Object | Sort-Object Count -Descending | Select-Object Name, Count | Format-Table -AutoSize
Write-Host "Report written to $OutputPath" -ForegroundColor Green
```

## How to run

1. Run it on a small test library first. Compare five files by hand with what the browser shows in the file details pane.
2. Run it with your real `-AllowedLabels`. Type the label names exactly as they appear in Purview, including spaces; the comparison ignores upper and lower case but nothing else.
3. Add `-ReviewField` only when the column exists with that internal name, and `-CheckApprovalStatus` only when content approval is on.
4. Hand the CSV to the document owners with the one-line rule: every file needs a label from the list, and review dates are not in the past.

## Worked example (invented data)

A library has 240 files. The script reports: 18 with NoRetentionLabel, 6 with LabelNotAllowed (an old label that was replaced), 31 with ReviewOverdue, 4 with NoReviewDate. One file can appear in several groups, so the sum of the counts (59) is higher than the number of flagged files, which is 52 in this example. The 18 unlabelled files are 7.5 percent of 240. The sensible first step is not to label them in bulk: an owner confirms the document type per folder, and then the compliance team applies the matching label by policy. The numbers are invented.

## How to adapt

- Several libraries: loop over titles and append `Library` to each row.
- Extra checks: no check-in comment, last change older than your review period, file type outside an allowed list. Add them as further `$issues`.
- Supplier certificates: add the expiry date column as `-ReviewField` and treat overdue as expired.
- Remediation: the script does not apply labels. Use label policies or auto-apply in Microsoft Purview where the rule can be written down, or ask owners to apply labels with an agreed list. A bulk script that changes labels belongs behind a separate review with the records manager.

## Common mistakes

- Using display names for columns. `Get-PnPListItem -Fields` and `FieldValues` use internal names.
- Typing allowed labels with different spelling and getting hundreds of false positives.
- Reading "no label" as "no retention". Tenant-wide retention policies may apply without a label; check what the policies do.
- Ignoring that a label can be applied by policy later. The report is a snapshot.
- Treating the review date as proof of review. It is a value somebody typed; the review itself is evidenced by your process.

## Privacy and security

- File names and paths can be sensitive. Treat the CSV like the library: restricted audience, deleted per your retention rules.
- No secrets in the script, no tokens in logs. Interactive sign-in only; for scheduled runs use a certificate-based app registration with read-only access to the site.
- The report names no people. If you add `Editor` or `Author` columns, tell the works council or data protection officer first.
